cards.text: Paul is writing to God's people in Rome (Romans 1:1, 7), and he's just told them they've been made right with God through Jesus (Romans 5:1). Now he goes all the way back to Adam, the first man (Genesis 2:7). Sin came into the world through that one man, and death came in through sin.

cards.question: Sin came in through one man, and death came in through sin. According to Paul, who does death pass on to?

answers.text: Only the man who sinned first

cards.text: Paul says sin was in the world before the law was given, but sin isn't taken into account when there's no law. It's like speeding down a road before anybody puts up the sign: still too fast, but nothing to write on the ticket.

cards.question: Even with no law to count sin, death didn't take a day off. Paul says death reigned from Adam until which man?
From Adam to Moses, Israel's leader, death reigned even over people who didn't sin the way Adam did.

cards.text: Then Paul calls Adam a pattern of the One to come. Now you're speaking my language, friend: I'm a stamper, and patterns are my WHOLE job.

cards.question: Paul calls Adam a pattern of the One to come. Who is that One?
Paul puts Adam's trespass next to the gift that comes through Jesus. The gift is just like the trespass.
The many died by one man's trespass. In Paul's comparison, which one goes further?

cards.text: Paul's still comparing, and now he's counting, like me checking cookie boxes at closing time. The judgment brought condemnation, and the gift brought justification.

cards.question: The judgment that followed ___ sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed ___ trespasses brought justification.

cards.text: Then Paul says by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man. ONE man, and death's walking around like it owns the place.

cards.question: Paul says those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through Jesus Christ.

cards.text: Now Paul ties the whole thing up like a cookie box. One trespass brought condemnation for all men.

cards.question: One trespass brought condemnation for all men. According to Paul, what brought justification and life for all men?
The many were made sinners through Adam's ___, and the many will be made righteous through Jesus' ___.

cards.text: Then Paul brings the law back into the picture, and he tells us what it came in for. Lean in, friend. This one's worth the wait.

cards.question: Paul says the law came in so that the trespass would shrink.
The law came in so that the trespass would increase. What did grace do where sin increased?
Paul lands it: just as ___ reigned in death, so also ___ might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

findings.problem: The right answer 'All people because all sinned' is the only one that adds a reason clause. Both wrong answers start with 'Only', so the right answer is the odd one out and stands out by its form, not its meaning.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Blank 1 is followed by the singular 'sin'. 'three sin', 'seven sin' and 'few sin' are ungrammatical, so 'one' is the only word that fits and the baker can get it from grammar alone. Card 10 also says Paul is 'counting', which together with the number options points straight at the answer. The wrong options need to fit both blanks grammatically.

findings.problem: This story card is not the opening card but has three sentences ('Then Paul brings the law back...', 'Lean in, friend.', 'This one's worth the wait.').

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The hype lines 'Lean in, friend. This one's worth the wait.' are filler with no real laugh. This verse is a natural setup for a big reaction: the law came in so the trespass would increase. Instead, the card reads like a pleasant teaser.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: 'Now Paul ties the whole thing up like a cookie box' is a mild, pleasant comparison with no punch. Paul's 'So then' summary (one trespass vs one act of righteousness) could hold a real laugh.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
